Learning Objectives
Discuss the epidemiology, etiology, and factors associated with distal triceps injuries.
Describe the physical examination findings and imaging studies used to diagnose distal triceps
injuries.
Review nonsurgical and surgical treatment options for the management of distal triceps
injuries.
Outline the postoperative protocol for patients who undergo distal triceps tendon repair and
review expected outcomes of nonsurgical and surgical management of distal triceps injuries.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview

Distal triceps injuries are rare and most commonly result from trauma in men in their forties
or fifties.
Injuries may be partial or complete tears near the tendon-bone interface at the olecranon.
Partial tears may recover via a course of nonsurgical management.
Complete tears generally are managed surgically.

Overview
Distal triceps injuries are rare compared with other tendon injuries. They most
commonly occur in men in their forties or fifties and usually are associated with a large
eccentric load with elbow extension. Bilateral ruptures may occur and are more common
in those who use anabolic steroids. Partial ruptures may occur within the midsubstance
of the tendon. Nonsurgical management of partial ruptures occasionally is successful;
however, patients may experience continued weakness. Except in rare circumstances,
complete tears of the tendon always are managed via surgical repair. Although multiple
repair constructs have been described, no one construct has been associated with
improved clinical results based on limited data.
Epidemiology
Rare condition constituting less than 1% of all tendon ruptures
Most common in males in their forties and fifties
Male to female ratio is 3:2 in individuals in their thirties

Epidemiology
Distal triceps ruptures are rare injuries, accounting for less than 1% of all tendon
ruptures and approximately 3% of elbow tendon injuries.1 Lateral and medial
epicondylitis are the most common elbow tendon injuries, followed by distal biceps
injuries and distal triceps injuries. Men in their forties fifties are more commonly affected
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:00 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002020
2/28

than women. Anabolic steroid use and systemic diseases, such as chronic renal failure,
rheumatoid arthritis, and diabetes mellitus, increase the risk for distal triceps injuries.
Anatomy and Biomechanics
The mean length of the superficial triceps tendon, measured from the tip of the olecranon to
the most proximal extent of the tendon medially, is 15.2 cm (range, 13.3 to 17.1 cm).
The distal aspect of the extensor tendon is more expansive laterally, at which fibers of the
triceps fascia blend with the brachioradialis and the common wrist extensors. This lateral
triceps expansion is continuous with the superficial fascia of the anconeus muscle and the
antebrachial fascia inserting into the radial aspect of the proximal ulna distally.
The medial triceps tendon inserts directly into the medial aspect of the olecranon process
without expansion.
The medial aspect of the tendon is thicker than the lateral aspect and consistently shows a
distinct, thickened, rolled tendon edge medially.
The mean medial to lateral width of the tendon insertional footprint is 20.9 mm (or 78% of the
maximal width of the olecranon).
The mean length from the tip of the olecranon process to the most proximal aspect of the
tendon insertion near the curved apex of the olecranon is 14.8 mm.
The triceps brachii muscle is the primary extensor of the elbow joint.

Anatomy and Biomechanics
The triceps muscle consists of three heads that serve as the primary extensor of the
elbow joint and contribute to shoulder extension. The long head originates from the
infraglenoid tubercle, the medial head originates from the medial aspect of the humeral
shaft distal to the spiral groove of the humerus, and the lateral head originates from the
intermuscular septum and the lateral humeral shaft proximal to the spiral groove. The
three heads become confluent at the distal triceps tendon, which inserts on the
olecranon in a bilaminate fashion. The medial head contributes to the deeper portion of
the tendon attachment, and the lateral and long heads contribute to the more
superficial tendinous insertion. The muscle also has a broad and long tendon measuring
a mean of 15.2 cm from the tip of the olecranon to the most proximal portion medially.

9/3/26, 4:00 PM

3/28

The lateral portion distally is more expansive as it transitions into the fascia and tendons
of the common extensor tendons and the superficial fascia of the anconeus.2 The
tendon insertion is on the proximal ulna at the olecranon process, with a mean footprint
of 22 mm in length and 22 mm in width in a dome-type shape3 (Figure 1). The muscle is
innervated by the radial nerve as it travels through the spiral groove of the humerus. The
vascular supply is the deep brachial artery with distal contribution from the superior
ulnar collateral artery and proximal contribution from the posterior circumflex humeral
artery. (Resource 1)
Figure 1 Illustration shows the dome-shaped triceps insertion on the posterior
olecranon (outlined in red) after dissection. The distal triceps tendon should be repaired
to reapproximate this footprint. (Reproduced from Haverstock JP, Athwal GS:
Acute/traumatic elbow injuries, in Miller MD, ed: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Sports
Medicine, ed 5. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2016, pp 81-
90).

Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Most common mechanism of injury is a sudden eccentric load to a contracting triceps muscle,
such as a fall onto an outstretched arm.
Ruptures most commonly occur at the tendon-bone insertion; however, muscle belly ruptures
and tears at the musculotendinous junction also can occur.

Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
The two most common mechanisms of injury are traumatic in nature, being a fall onto a
flexed elbow with a forced eccentric extension or from weightlifting. Anabolic steroid use
in weightlifters increases the risk for tendon rupture and is associated with bilateral
ruptures. More rarely, injury and traumatic tendon lacerations occur during sports, such
as football.4 Chronic ruptures also may occur and are commonly associated with
antecedent pain in the distal triceps followed by increasing pain or progressive
weakness. Partial tears may be associated with traumatic or chronic injuries. The most
common site of injury is an avulsion of the tendon insertion from the olecranon. Partial
tears may be more common in the deep portion of the tendon insertion from the medial
head. Midsubstance tendon ruptures, musculotendinous junction tears, and muscle
belly ruptures are less common.
Risk Factors
Predisposing factors include the following:
Olecranon bursitis
Local corticosteroid injections
Anabolic steroids
Type 1 diabetes mellitus
Rheumatoid arthritis
Metabolic bone diseases (hyperparathyroidism and renal osteodystrophy)

Risk Factors
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:00 PM
AAOS | Distal Triceps Tendon Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002020
5/28

Patient factors that may increase the risk for triceps tendon injuries include anabolic
steroid use; systemic inflammatory diseases, such as diabetes and rheumatoid arthritis;
and metabolic diseases, such as renal osteodystrophy from chronic renal failure and
hyperparathyroidism. Metabolic bone diseases are thought to increase the risk for
rupture by weakening the insertion site of the olecranon through osteoclastic bone
resorption.
Associated Injuries
Collateral ligament injuries
Ulnar neuropathy from hematoma
Olecranon fracture
Bilateral tears with anabolic steroid use

Associated Injuries
Associated injuries, including collateral ligament injuries about the elbow, have been
reported in patients with a traumatic rupture of the triceps tendon. Rare occurrences of
concomitant olecranon fractures and ulnar nerve palsy caused by hematoma formation
after the injury have been reported.5 Anabolic steroid use is a known risk factor for
bilateral tendon ruptures.
Injury Classification
Full-thickness tendon tear
Partial-thickness tendon tear
Chronic triceps tendinosis
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002020
6/28

Patients may recall a popping sound or a tearing sensation at the time of injury.
Patients report pain, swelling, and bruising along the posterior elbow.
Delayed presentation is common if some motion and strength is preserved.
Patients report numbness or tingling in the ulnar nerve distribution, particularly if they present
with a concomitant hematoma.

Patient History
Because most distal triceps injuries are traumatic in nature, most patients will present
with a history of trauma, such as a fall onto the injured extremity or a pop or tearing
sound when lifting a heavy weight while extending the elbow. The patient will notice pain
in the posterior elbow, weakness with attempted elbow extension, and bruising that
develops a day or two after injury about the posterior elbow. Patients with partial tears
may seek care days to weeks after the initial injury because of persistent pain and slight
weakness. Those patients will continue to maintain active motion and most strength but
will note continued pain with resisted elbow extension. Rarely, numbness and tingling
may be noted in the ring and little finger because of hematoma formation and
compression of the ulnar nerve.
Physical Examination
Tenderness to palpation over the posterior aspect of the elbow; a palpable defect of the
tendon proximal to the olecranon may or may not be present (Figure 2).
Passive motion usually is preserved; however, active extension may be compromised or
present, depending on the degree of rupture. With complete ruptures, inability to actively
extend against resistance/gravity is pathognomonic for a complete rupture.
Positive modified Thompson squeeze test may confirm complete triceps rupture.
An intact lateral expansion may mask the common physical examination findings indicative of
acute triceps ruptures. Therefore, surgeons must maintain a high index of suspicion to avoid
misdiagnosis.

7/28

Figure 2 Sagittal T2-weighted MRI of an elbow shows a complete tear of the distal triceps
tendon. (Reproduced from Baumfeld JA, Tolo ET: Triceps tendon repair, in Ring DC, Steinmann
SP, eds: Advanced Reconstruction: Elbow, ed 2. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic
Surgeons, 2016, pp 59-65.)

Physical Examination
The contralateral extremity should be examined first to evaluate a patient’s normal
range of motion and strength. Physical examination of the injured extremity will reveal
possible ecchymosis about the posterior elbow and swelling posteriorly. Palpation of the
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:00 PM
AAOS | Distal Triceps Tendon Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002020
8/28

elbow will reveal tenderness posteriorly. In patients with a complete tear, a defect can be
palpated in the triceps tendon just proximal to the tip of the olecranon. Passive range of
motion with flexion and extension generally is preserved; however, slight pain may be
present posteriorly at the end range of flexion. Active motion with flexion should not be
affected; however, considerable pain and weakness likely will be present with resisted
extension or against gravity. If medial and lateral tendon expansions are maintained, the
patient may exhibit active extension against gravity but considerable weakness against
resistance. Similar to Achilles tendon ruptures, the modified Thompson test may be
positive if the triceps muscle belly is squeezed and no passive extension of the elbow
occurs.6 In general, neurovascular examination is maintained. Rarely, patients may
exhibit ulnar nerve–related symptoms, with ulnar numbness in the hand if a
considerable hematoma is compressing the ulnar nerve (Resource 2).
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Standard radiographs (AP and lateral views) of the elbow should be obtained. A fleck sign
observed on a lateral radiograph is pathognomonic for an avulsion fracture/triceps rupture.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRIs may be used for preoperative planning, in patients in whom determination of a partial or
complete rupture is difficult, and patients in whom localization of the exact location of a tear is
difficult (Figure 3).

Figure 3 Clinical photograph of the elbow of a patient with a distal triceps rupture shows a
palpable defect proximal to the olecranon. The abrasion just distal to the olecranon indicates
the area of impact during injury, (Reproduced from Yeh PC, Dodds SD, Smart LR, Mazzocca AD,
Sethi PM: Distal triceps rupture. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2010;18[1]:31-40.) 
Ultrasonography
Ultrasonography is operator dependent but less expensive and may be useful.

Imaging Studies
Initial radiographs include AP and lateral views of the elbow. Lateral radiographs may
demonstrate specific findings, most notably a fleck sign (Dunn-Kusnezov sign) if a
small portion of the olecranon is avulsed and displaced, which is pathognomonic for a
distal triceps tendon tear7 (Figure 4). In patients with chronic posterior elbow pain, a
traction enthesophyte, which may or may not be fractured and displaced from
traumatic injury, may be observed on lateral radiographs. If the patient history and
physical examination findings are consistent with a distal triceps injury, MRI regularly
is obtained to confirm the diagnosis and evaluate the nature of the tendon injury
(partial- versus full-thickness injury). In addition, chronic injuries may necessitate MRI
to evaluate the quality of the tendon and the degree of retraction to determine if
allograft augmentation may be required. If a patient is averse to MRI, ultrasonography
may be performed to confirm the diagnosis and determine additional characteristics
of the tendon tear.

sign (arrow), which indicates an injury to the triceps tendon insertion. MRI is
warranted to fully appreciate the extent of the injury. (Reproduced from Ahmad CS,
Irvine JN Jr: Malignant primary bone tumor, in Parvizi J, ed: Orthopaedic Knowledge
Update, ed 13. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2021, pp
353-363).
Differential Diagnosis
Full-thickness triceps tendon tear
Partial-thickness triceps tendon tear
Chronic triceps tendinosis
Symptomatic traction olecranon enthesophyte
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Indications
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:00 PM
AAOS | Distal Triceps Tendon Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002020
11/28

Partial and/or complete tears in debilitated, elderly patients may be managed nonsurgically.
Anatomic factors also contribute to treatment decision making.
Tear location
Muscle belly tears tend to heal with scar tissue rather than newly regenerated muscle.
Partial ruptures at tendon-osseous insertion often do not heal and result in persistent pain.
Partial tears comprising less than 50% of tendon width can be managed nonsurgically with
satisfactory results. Tears larger than 50% in active individuals may require surgical
management.
Complete tears usually are managed surgically.
Incomplete tendon rupture should be managed initially via a trial of nonsurgical management.
Good return to preinjury level is possible, even in high-demand athletes with a partial tear.

Indications
Partial tears of the triceps tendon may be managed initially via a course of nonsurgical
management. Patients most likely to do well with nonsurgical treatment include those
with tears comprising less than 50% of tendon width and patients with lower demands.
The location of the tear also may portend better results with nonsurgical management,
with muscle belly tears generally healing well without surgical management. Tendon
tears at the tendon-bone junction are less likely to heal and, therefore, may result in
continued pain if not repaired. Although partial tears larger than 50% of tendon width
and full-thickness tears in younger, active individuals result in greater improvement with
surgical fixation, older, more sedentary patients with similar injuries may progress well
without surgical treatment.8
Surgical Management
Indications
Surgical management is indicated for acute, complete tears, particularly at the distal tendinous
insertion patients with of loss of active extension against gravity.
Surgical management also should be considered in younger, active patients with a partial tear
in whom a course of nonsurgical treated fails.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:00 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002020
12/28

Contraindications
Acute infection of the elbow
Open traumatic injury
Techniques/Procedures
Preoperative Planning
A thorough physical examination to evaluate the symptoms and extent of swelling, soft-tissue
envelope, and strength
Imaging studies (plain radiographs and advanced imaging studies) to define the injury
Plain radiographs will demonstrate any olecranon enthesophyte that may require excision at
the time of surgery.
A fleck sign may be observed and generally is pathognomonic for a triceps tendon tear.
MRI usually is performed to define the extent of the tendon tear, the location of the tendon
tear, and quality of the tendon.

Preoperative Planning
The physical examination should begin with an evaluation of the uninjured elbow to
assess for normal size, contours, and strength of the patient. Physical examination of the
injured elbow should then begin with inspection, noting any swelling, ecchymosis, skin
breakdown, or dimpling posteriorly. Palpation of the elbow should focus on the bony
epicondyles medially and laterally and the olecranon process posteriorly. The biceps
tendon should be palpated anteriorly to confirm integrity. The triceps tendon may then
be palpated posteriorly. In patients with a complete rupture, a gap will be felt just
proximal to the tip of the olecranon. A modified Thompson test is performed by
squeezing the triceps muscle belly and assessing motion at the elbow. In patients with a
complete rupture, no extension of the elbow will occur. Strength testing in flexion,
extension, pronation, and supination is assessed. Patients with a partial rupture will be
able to mount resistance to extension but with pain. Patients with a complete rupture
usually will have strength rated three out of five or less and likely will have pain with
resisted extension.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:00 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002020
13/28

Imaging studies are obtained, with plain radiographs obtained to rule out fractures,
specifically of the olecranon process. Often, radiographs will appear unremarkable;
however, an olecranon traction enthesophyte, which may be fractured with the injury,
may be observed. In patients without an enthesophyte, a small fleck of olecranon may
be displaced proximally (Dunn-Kusnezov sign), which is pathognomonic for a triceps
tendon injury. If a triceps tendon rupture is suspected, MRI generally is performed to
confirm the diagnosis and evaluate the degree of rupture. In addition, MRI may aid in
assessing the quality of the tendon and the potential need for graft to augment the
repair.
Patient Positioning
Supine with a bump under the shoulder and the arm draped over the body
Lateral decubitus position with the injured arm on an arm holder (Figure 5) 
Figure 5 Intraoperative photograph shows a patient placed in the lateral decubitus position,
with the right elbow placed in an arm holder. (Reproduced from Baumfeld JA, Tolo ET: Triceps
tendon repair, in Ring DC, Steinmann SP, eds: Advanced Reconstruction: Elbow, ed 2. Rosemont,

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002020
14/28

IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2016, pp 59-65.)

Patient Positioning
The patient may be placed in two different positions to adequately access the posterior
aspect of the elbow. The patient may be placed in the supine position with a small bump
under the shoulder blade and the arm draped across the body, with a sterile bump on
the anterior aspect of the elbow. The arm may be held in position by clamping the sterile
stockinette to the drapes or having an assistant hold the arm. A potential advantage of
this position is avoiding endotracheal intubation and potential pressure points from
lateral positioning.
Alternatively, the patient may be placed in the lateral decubitus position, with the injured
side up and the arm positioned on an arm holder. In this position, the down leg must be
well padded, specifically at the greater trochanter of the hip and the peroneal nerve at
the knee. An advantage of this position is that it is less reliant on an assistant to hold the
arm during the procedure.
The arm may be prepared with or without a sterile or nonsterile tourniquet based on
surgeon preference. In patients with a large, retracted tear or in whom a graft may be
necessary, the tourniquet may need to be let down or removed for mobilization of the
muscle.
Surgical Approach and Technique
An open posterior approach is used, with medial and lateral skin flaps, and the triceps tendon
is directly identified.
Various fixation techniques have been described, with no strong evidence supporting one
fixation technique over another.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:00 PM
AAOS | Distal Triceps Tendon Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002020
15/28

Heavy, nonabsorbable sutures are passed through the tendon and attached to the olecranon
with transosseous tunnels.
Suture anchors placed in the olecranon; sutures passed through the tendon and tied to
repair the tendon may be single row or double row.
Hybrid of transosseous tunnels with knotless suture anchor repair
Reconstruction
For chronic tears, advancement of the tendon to the olecranon may not be possible.
An Achilles tendon allograft may be used to reconstruct the triceps.
A hamstring allograft weave through the distal triceps and transosseous olecranon is another
option.
Direct repair through bone tunnels
Suture anchor repair
Hybrid bone tunnel and anchor repair
Reconstruction with Achilles tendon allograft

Surgical Approach and Technique
The posterior approach to the elbow is used to access the triceps tendon and perform
the repair. Being a subcutaneous muscle and tendon, a skin incision is made centrally in
the brachium posteriorly, extended distally to the lateral aspect of the olecranon and
approximately 3 to 4 cm distally over the subcutaneous border of the ulna. The incision
is carried sharply to the fascia of the triceps and the paratenon of the tendon, and
medial and lateral skin flaps are raised. Caution should be exercised in raising the medial
skin flap to avoid injury to the ulnar nerve, the position of which should be identified and
protected (Figure 6). At this point, the tendon tear usually is easily visualized, except for
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:00 PM
AAOS | Distal Triceps Tendon Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002020
16/28

some partial tears, which may consist of the deeper tendon fibers. The paratenon should
then be incised and dissected from the tendon medially and laterally to aid in layered
closure after the repair. The periosteum of the olecranon and the subcutaneous border
of the ulna should be incised and raised to expose the bony surfaces. The torn edges of
the tendon should be debrided of any necrotic tissue and prepared for direct repair to
the bone.

which lies just medial to the torn triceps tendon. (Reproduced from Baumfeld JA, Tolo ET:
Triceps tendon repair, in Ring DC, Steinmann SP, eds: Advanced Reconstruction: Elbow, ed
2. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2016, pp 59-65.)
Many techniques have been described to repair the tendon to the bone, with no one
technique demonstrating improved results over another.
Two heavy, nonabsorbable sutures are woven in a locking, Krackow fashion through the
torn edge of the tendon to leave four strands exiting the distal portion of the tendon.
Three parallel tunnels or two cruciate tunnels are then drilled through the olecranon
process in an antegrade fashion. If three parallel tunnels are being used, one limb from
each suture is passed through the central tunnel and one each on the medial and lateral
tunnels. If cruciate tunnels are being used, caution should be exercised to ensure that
the passing device does not spear or interfere with the sutures as they cross. One limb
from each suture is then passed through opposing tunnels, and the sutures are tied over
the bony bridge. The knots should be tied on the lateral or medial surface of the ulna
rather than directly over the subcutaneous portion to avoid irritation of the knots when
resting the elbow down (Figure 7).

technique for triceps tendon repair. A, Locking sutures are used to grasp the tendon for
a four-strand repair. B, Sutures are passed through bone tunnels in the olecranon. C,
The triceps tendon is delivered to the bone, and sutures are tied. (Reproduced from
Baumfeld JA, Tolo ET: Triceps tendon repair, in Ring DC, Steinmann SP, eds: Advanced

Multiple suture repair techniques have been described for single-row repair or double-
row footprint repair. In the single-row technique, two anchors are placed in the posterior
aspect of the olecranon angling away from the joint. One limb from each suture is woven
in a locking Krackow fashion through the tendon, and one limb is passed through in a
simple, sliding fashion. The sutures are then tied down, using the simple limb as the post
to compress the tendon to bone. (Figure 8; Videos 1 and 2).
Figure 8 Intraoperative photographs of an elbow show steps in the anchor technique for
triceps tendon repair. A, The sutures are passed through two bone anchors. B, The
anchors are placed into the olecranon at the triceps footprint. C, The appearance of the
final repair with the lateral triceps tendon sutured to the intact anconeus. (Reproduced
from Baumfeld JA, Tolo ET: Triceps tendon repair, in Ring DC, Steinmann SP, eds:
Advanced Reconstruction: Elbow, ed 2. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic
Surgeons, 2016, pp 59-65.)

In the double-row technique, the same method is used proximally to secure the tendon
to the bone or the sutures are tied in a horizontal mattress fashion and a free suture is
woven in a Krackow fashion before the suture anchors are tied. Regardless, the sutures
are tied approximately 2 to 3 cm proximal to the end of the tendon. The suture limbs are
then brought into a knotless suture anchor and fixed into the ulna distal from the tip of
the olecranon. This technique helps to compress and re-create the broad insertional
footprint of the tendon onto the olecranon (Resource 3).
In this technique bone tunnels and a single knotless anchor are used, which creates a
footprint-type repair. Two heavy, nonabsorbable braided sutures are woven through the
tendon in a locking Krackow fashion. All four limbs should exit the tendon distally. Two
sutures with looped ends are then passed through the tendon 2 to 3 cm proximal to the
torn end, with the looped end proximal and superficial and the nonlooped end deep and
distal. Two parallel tunnels are then drilled through the olecranon. The two limbs of the
medial suture and the free end of the medially looped suture are passed through the
medial tunnel, which is then repeated laterally. One limb from the medial suture is then
passed laterally through the looped suture. This brings this limb back over the posterior
aspect of the tendon and exits the lateral tunnel. This is repeated on the opposite side.
All four limbs are then loaded into a knotless suture anchor, compressed, and secured in
the subcutaneous shaft of the ulna. This compresses the tendon along the footprint
without leaving knots on the repaired surface and limits the number of anchors needed
for repair.
In patients with a chronic tendon injury, poor-quality tendon and/or retraction and
scarring of the muscle may preclude advancement of the tendon to the olecranon. In
such patients, an Achilles tendon allograft may be used to reconstruct the chronic tear.
Patient positioning and the approach are similar to those used for acute repair. Two
options are available to secure the tendon to the bone, depending on the quality of the
olecranon bone. If adequate bone stock is present, the Achilles tendon graft can be
secured to the triceps as described. The appropriate length of tendon is selected and

trimmed, and the graft tendon is secured in a manner similar to that for primary repair.
If inadequate or poor-quality olecranon bone stock is present, the calcaneal portion of
the graft may be fashioned to sit on the volar-proximal portion of the olecranon. This is
then secured via a tension band technique or a screw. The appropriate length to tension
relationship is selected with the elbow in 40° to 60° of flexion, and the graft is secured to
the triceps.
The Achilles tendon graft can be woven through the tendonous portion of the triceps in
a Pulvertaft fashion, leaving the expanse of the Achilles tendon graft posteriorly over the
triceps muscle. The Pulvertaft weave is secured with the use of No. 2 nonabsorbable
suture, and the Achilles tendon expansion is secured in a burrito fashion around the
muscle.9
Postoperative Management
Immobilization in an anterior splint in 30° of flexion for 10 to 14 days postoperatively to
decrease tension on the repair.
The splint is removed at the first postoperative visit. Active-assisted flexion range of motion is
initiated, beginning with a 90° flexion block and advancing 10° per week for 4 weeks. Only
passive extension is permitted to avoid stress on the repair.
At 6 weeks postoperatively, light strengthening with extension is initiated and continued for 6
weeks.
At 12 weeks postoperatively, strengthening is advanced, with the goal to advance to
unrestricted activity at 4 to 6 months postoperatively.
Most patients who undergo acute primary repair regain near full strength but may lose 5° to
10° of full extension.

The goal of postoperative rehabilitation is to protect the repair while allowing for early,
progressive range of motion of the elbow. Immediately postoperatively, the a splint is
applied. An anterior splint folded into a T-shape is preferred because it results in less
skin incision irritation and provides more stability to protect against flexion. The patient
is seen approximately 10 to 14 days postoperatively for wound assessment and splint
removal. A hinged elbow brace is fitted with a block at 90° of flexion and no block with
extension. Physical therapy is initiated with active assisted flexion and passive extension.
No limits are placed on extension. Flexion is limited to 90° initially and progressed 10°
per week for 4 weeks. The patient is seen at 6 weeks postoperatively, at which time use
of the elbow brace can be discontinued. Progressive active-assisted range of motion is
continued with gentle strengthening with flexion and extension. At 3 months
postopertively, the patient can progress to full strength in extension, with the goal of
advancement to unrestricted activity by 4 to 6 months postoperatively, depending on the
patient’s activity level or sport
Pitfalls and Preventative Measures
Although the ulnar nerve does not need to be formally dissected and mobilized in patients
without preoperative symptoms, its location should be identified and protected while working
on the medial aspect of the elbow.
Anchors placed in the subcutaneous border of the ulna should be angled distally to avoid a
breach into the articular surface.
Complications
Possible complications include: re-tear, olecranon bursitis, weakness with an extension lag,
decreased range of motion and/or function, irritation from underlying internal structures
which may require revision surgery, flexion/extension contractures, poor wound healing,
infection, and ulnar nerve dysfunction.

Rehabilitation
The course of nonsurgical management should include a limited period of
immobilization in a sling until acute pain is controlled, usually no more than 1 to 2
weeks. Physical therapy is then progressed to include passive and active-assisted range
of motion of the elbow, avoiding heavy extension resistance for 12 weeks.
Outcomes
Nonsurgical management
Outcomes in the literature are limited to small cohorts and case reports, with reasonable
outcomes reported in appropriately selected patients.
Nonsurgical management is more likely to fail in high-level patients participating in contact
sports.
Surgical management
Surgical fixation frequently is successful with regard to regaining strength and function of the
elbow.
A common complication is lack of full elbow range of motion.
Re-rupture is less common, occurring in approximately 6% of patients.
Most published outcomes are presented in case series, with varying reported outcomes.
A large systematic review of 40 studies that included 262 patients reported three main
conclusions:
Renal disease and anabolic steroid use are the most common comorbid conditions
associated with distal triceps rupture.
A fleck sign was observed on lateral radiographs in 61% of the patients, with inconsistent
reporting.
89% of patients return to normal pre-injury activity levels.

Outcomes
Many distal triceps injuries, although rare, are managed surgically, especially if they are
full-thickness injuries. Because of the rarity of the pathology, studies are limited to case
reports and case series. A recent systematic review evaluated 40 studies that included
262 patients. A high rate of success (89%) was reported with regard to return to preinjury
level of activity. In addition, a re-rupture rate of 6% was reported. Anabolic steroid use
and comorbid renal disease were major contributing factors to tendon rupture. The
radiographic fleck sign was observed in 61% of the patients, which was thought to be
pathognomonic; however, reporting was in consisted; with less reliable studies excluded,
the frequency of the radiographic fleck sign increased to 88%.10
A large retrospective cohort study published in 2018 reviewed 178 cases of acute triceps
repair to compare outcomes and complications between patients treated via anchor
repair versus transosseous tunnel repair. Of the procedures performed, 105 were
transosseous tunnel repairs and 73 were anchor repairs. Re-rupture rates of 6.7% and
zero were reported in the transosseous tunnel group and the anchor group,
respectively. The overall revision surgery rate was 9.5% in the transosseous group and
1.4% in the anchor group. Although good outcomes were reported in the transosseous
group, the study suggested improved outcomes in the anchor repair group11 (Resource
4).
